title: Sovereigns 2025 Transition and Default Study
text:
### Rating Transitions

Overview Total sovereign rating activity, defined as the combined share of upgrades and downgrades, remained elevated in 2025 but moderated slightly from the prior year. In 2025, 27 issuers experienced a rating transition, equivalent to 22.88% of the 118 issuers, compared with 28 issuers, or 24.56%, in 2024. Upgrades continued to drive the majority of actions, with 18 upgrades in 2025 (an upgrade rate of 15.25%) compared to 19 upgrades in 2024 (16.67%). Downgrades were unchanged in absolute terms at nine issuers, though the downgrade rate edged down slightly to 7.63% from 7.89% in 2024. The resulting downgrade-to-upgrade ratio was 0.50x in 2025, which was broadly consistent with 0.47x in 2024 and well below levels observed during periods of heightened stress. For historical context within the last decade, 2020 marked the most severe imbalance, when downgrades reached 27.12% (32 downgrades) compared to upgrades of 1.69% (two upgrades), which pushed the down-to-up ratio to 16.0x. Rating Activity by Region Regional patterns in 2025 show that rating activity was concentrated in Europe and, to a lesser extent, the Middle East and Africa. Europe recorded the highest number of actions, with eight upgrades and four downgrades, accounting for a meaningful share of both upgrade and downgrade volume. The Middle East and Africa followed with five upgrades and two downgrades, while Latin America recorded four upgrades and two downgrades. Asia Pacific saw limited activity, with one upgrade and one downgrade, and North America recorded no upgrades or downgrades. In aggregate, upgrades exceeded downgrades in every region where activity occurred, which aligns with the portfolio-wide down-to-up ratio remaining well below 1.0x for a second consecutive year. Rising Stars and Fallen Angels The number of ‘rising stars’ increased notably in 2025. Fitch Ratings recorded three rising stars (Aruba, Oman, and San Marino) and zero fallen angels during the year, compared to one rising star and one fallen angel in 2024. This shift is consistent with the broader pattern of positive net rating momentum and suggests that, within the transition cohort, upward migration into investment grade was more prevalent than downward migration out of investment grade.

Sovereign defaults fell to zero in 2025, with no Fitch-rated sovereign issuers defaulting during the 
year. As a result, the annual default rate was 0.0%, down from 0.88% (one default) in 2024. The 
average annual default rate for the sovereign portfolio over 1995 to 2025 was 0.98%. 
Investment-grade sovereigns again recorded a 0.0% default rate in 2025, consistent with the period 
shown, and speculative-grade sovereigns also recorded a 0.0% default rate, an improvement from 
1.89% in 2024. The recent default cycle shown in the historical series highlights the extent of the 
improvement: annual default rates peaked at 4.24% in 2020, remained high in 2022 and 2023 at 
2.54% and 2.61%, then fell in 2024 and reached zero in 2025. 
Supranationals have continued to register no defaults over the historical period starting in 2004. 
Per Fitch’s methodology, the default rate is calculated based on issuers that were outstanding in the 
previous year and defaulted in the current year. Therefore, defaults occurring within the same year 
by newly rated issuers or issuers re-rated from default are not included in the cohort or default 
counts. 
The 2025 transition matrix provides additional confirmation of this outcome, showing no migration 
into default (D) and no withdrawals. In grouped terms, ‘AAA’, ‘A’, ‘BBB’, and ‘B’ cohorts each show 
100% of issuers remaining in their starting category. The ‘AA’ cohort shows 88.89% remaining in 
‘AA’ and 11.11% migrating to ‘A’, while the ‘BB’ cohort shows 88.89% remaining in ‘BB’ and 11.11% 
migrating to ‘BBB’. The ‘CCC’ to ‘C’ cohort shows more dispersion, with 72.73% remaining in ‘CCC’ 
to ‘C’ and 27.27% migrating to ‘B’, but still no transitions to default.

Overview The sovereign ratings portfolio expanded in 2025, and the rating mix shifted modestly. At year-end 2025, there were 124 sovereign ratings outstanding, up from 118 at year-end 2024. The average rating in 2025 was ‘BBB-’. The year-end 2025 distribution was led by the ‘BB’ and ‘B’ categories, each with 25 issuers (20.16% apiece), followed by ‘A’ with 21 issuers (16.94%) and ‘BBB’ with 18 issuers (14.52%). Higher-rated categories comprised 16 issuers in ‘AA’ (12.90%) and nine in ‘AAA’ (7.26%), while the lowest categories (‘CCC’ to ‘C’) accounted for 10 issuers (8.06%). Relative to year-end 2024, the most notable changes were an increase in ‘B’ (from 19 to 25) as well as increases in ‘A’ (from 19 to 21) and ‘BBB’ (from 15 to 18), alongside declines in ‘AA’ (from 18 to 16), ‘BB’ (from 27 to 25), and ‘CCC’ to ‘C’ (from 11 to 10). There are 31 ratings outstanding in the supranationals ratings portfolio. With most ratings having been affirmed in 2025, the average rating remained at ‘AA’. Regional Overview The regional distribution of sovereign ratings at year-end 2025 remained broad-based, with Europe continuing to represent the largest share of the portfolio. Europe accounted for 43 issuers (34.68%), followed by the Middle East and Africa with 35 issuers (28.23%), Asia Pacific with 24 issuers (19.35%), Latin America with 20 issuers (16.13%), and North America with two issuers (1.61%). The detailed regional rating distribution illustrates meaningful differences in rating profiles across regions. Europe had the widest spread across the rating spectrum, including seven issuers in ‘AAA’, five in ‘AA’, 15 in ‘A’, eight in ‘BBB,’ six in ‘BB’, and smaller representation in the lower categories. Asia Pacific combined a meaningful high-grade component, including two issuers in ‘AAA’ and five issuers in ‘AA’, with representation across ‘A’, ‘BBB’, ‘BB’, ‘B’, and ‘CCC’ to ’CC’. The Middle East and Africa region was more concentrated in speculative grade, with 17 issuers in ‘B’ (48.57% of the region’s total) and seven issuers in ‘BB’, while still maintaining some higher-rated issuers (including four in ‘AA’ and three in ‘A’). Latin America was concentrated in ‘BB’ (nine issuers) and included four in ‘BBB’, three in ‘B’, and three in ‘CCC’, underscoring its predominantly speculative-grade profile. North America’s two sovereigns were both in the ‘AA’ category.

### Fitch-Rated Sovereigns IDR Defaults (2010–2025)

Jamaica (2010): A distressed debt exchange (DDE) in February 2010 affected the country’s domestic debt, which included foreign currency (FC)-denominated instruments to which Fitch’s FC rating applied (FC and Local Currency [LC] Issuer Default Ratings [IDRs]). Greece (2012): A DDE in March 2012 affected about EUR199 billion of Greek and foreign law government bonds and resulted in each EUR100 face value amount of Greek government bonds being exchanged for new bonds (FC and LC IDRs). Jamaica (2013): A DDE in February 2013 included JMD860 billion in FC and LC domestic debt, and resulted in FC and LC IDR downgrades to ‘RD’. The DDE announced by the government included the extension of maturities and a reduction in coupons for the affected debt instruments. The debt exchange was one of the preconditions for Jamaica to sign a new International Monetary Fund (IMF) agreement totaling nearly USD750 million (FC and LC IDRs). Cyprus (2013): A DDE in June 2013 comprised an exchange of domestic government bonds, which resulted in a downgrade of the LC IDR to ‘RD’. The exchange involved domestic bonds with a total nominal value of EUR1 billion that were due to mature within the EU-IMF program period from 2013 to 1Q16. These bonds were replaced by new bonds carrying the same coupon rates but with maturity dates extended beyond the original program period. As foreign Cypriot bonds were unaffected, the FC IDR remained unchanged (LC IDR). Argentina (2014): A missed-payment default occurred on discount bonds issued under foreign law following the expiration of the 30-day grace period. The default related to a dispute between Argentina and certain holdout creditors that did not participate in the 2005 and 2010 exchange offers, which culminated in the denial of Argentina’s certiorari petition to the U.S. Supreme Court. The U.S. Lower Court ruling was upheld, prohibiting Argentina from making payments to exchanged bondholders unless payments were also made to the plaintiffs in the case (FC IDR). Ukraine (2015): There was a missed payment on Ukraine’s USD500 million eurobond maturing on September 23, 2015. The following day, Ukraine launched an exchange offer for about USD18 billion in direct and government-guaranteed eurobonds, which Fitch considered a DDE, resulting in a downgrade of the FC IDR to ‘RD’ (FC IDR). Republic of Congo (2016): The Republic of Congo missed a capital and interest payment on its U.S. dollar-denominated notes due 2029, which were issued under a restructuring of London Club debt in 2007. The rating was downgraded to ‘RD’ in August 2016 (FC IDR). Mozambique (2016): A missed capital and interest payment on a USD535 million loan to the state owned enterprise Mozambique Asset Management, guaranteed by the sovereign, resulted in a downgrade to ‘RD’ in November 2016 (FC IDR).

Republic of Congo (2017): Similar to its 2016 default, the Republic of Congo missed a capital and interest payment on its U.S. dollar-denominated notes due 2029 after funds were frozen due to legal proceedings.
